volunteer_experience.info: Cruzing Forward started with a scholarship and a simple belief: talent is everywhere, but opportunity isn't. I founded the Cruzing Forward Scholarship with $200 out of my own pocket, meant for students who reminded me of myself, first-gen, underrepresented, and figuring it all out without a roadmap. Person after person stepped up to match donations, and in a matter of days it grew to $1,000 and 300+ applicants, awarded to two incredible students. I documented the whole thing publicly… Show more Cruzing Forward started with a scholarship and a simple belief: talent is everywhere, but opportunity isn't. I founded the Cruzing Forward Scholarship with $200 out of my own pocket, meant for students who reminded me of myself, first-gen, underrepresented, and figuring it all out without a roadmap. Person after person stepped up to match donations, and in a matter of days it grew to $1,000 and 300+ applicants, awarded to two incredible students. I documented the whole thing publicly, episode by episode, because I wanted people to see that generosity is contagious when someone goes first. But Cruzing Forward was never just a scholarship. I have now built it into a community, sharing tech opportunities, advice, and encouragement with first-gen and underrepresented students. I've helped 5000+ students one on one and grown an audience of 3.5K+ across LinkedIn and Instagram, all rooted in one mission: making sure the next student doesn't have to figure it out alone the way I did. Now, I envision Cruzing Forward becoming a home where first-gen students find not just opportunities, but belonging. A place that connects students to scholarships, mentorship, and each other, and eventually creates the kinds of opportunities that don't exist yet. Access shouldn't depend on who you know or where you started. I'm building Cruzing Forward so it doesn't have to. Show less

publications.title: Commanding a Millennium Odyssey
publications.subtitle: Newbury Center (Elevate Magazine)
publications.description: My reflective essay “Commanding a Millennium Odyssey” appears in Elevate Magazine — Issue 4 “Journey,” published by Boston University’s Newbury Center for first-generation students (2025). In the piece, I trace my leap from home to college through the image of a fiery-orange sunset seen from an airplane window, wrestling with what it means to leave family, carry multiple identities, and redefine “success” beyond grades or titles. The story invites readers to embrace uncertainty, honor their roots, and craft a personal “story-truth” out of everyday moments of growth. Grateful to add my voice to the first-gen narrative and to keep turning dreams into goals on this continuing odyssey.

projects.title: Sapling
projects.description: Online interactive learning platform that turns every conversation into a structured knowledge map based on degrees of mastery, both academic and personal. Rather than requiring students to manually log their study material, Gemini automatically identifies and tracks concepts in real time, building a live graph of mastery as the session unfolds. The AI model establishes reinforced learning through relevant questioning and custom quizzes, rather than providing an immediate answer. Deadlines and assignments are tracked automatically with calendar authentication from uploaded syllabi and online assignment pages. A social comparison layer lets users view their knowledge tree alongside classmates, online members, or anyone at their school, enabling peer matching based on where each student's understanding diverges and active recall. Built with Next.js, FastAPI, D3.js, Supabase, and Google Gemini.

projects.title: Room Temperature Monitor (EK 131)
projects.description: The design report presents a portable, battery-powered room-temperature monitor that displays the current temperature on a 16 × 2 LCD screen and warns the user with a flashing red LED and piezo buzzer whenever the reading drifts outside a user-defined comfort band (e.g., 70 °F – 80 °F). This goal drives the entire engineering cycle documented in the report, from component selection through testing. At the heart of the prototype is an Arduino Uno, which reads an LM35 analog temperature sensor, drives the I²C LCD, and controls the alert system of LEDs and buzzer. All components are housed in a custom ABS enclosure; a neatly soldered harness collects common ground and 5 V rails, and jumpers route signals to the Arduino headers. Careful LED-current calculations (≈ 3 mA for the green power LED and ≈ 13 mA for the red alarm LED) balance brightness against battery life. Powered by a 9 V, 500 mAh battery regulated down to 5 V, the whole system draws about 70 mA, allowing roughly seven hours of continuous operation before the battery must be replaced or recharged.In operation, the sketch repeatedly samples the LM35, converts the voltage to degrees Fahrenheit, updates the display, and decides whether to trigger the audible-visual alarm. The sensor’s usable range spans –40 °F to 257 °F, and in the prototype the alarm band is set to 80 °F – 90 °F; the buzzer and LED activate immediately when readings leave this band and silence automatically when temperatures return to safe limits. Bench tests with a warm hand and a distant hair-dryer confirmed accurate readings and fast alarms, meeting all primary objectives, though the team notes battery life, weight, and enclosure size as areas for future refinement. Suggested improvements include swapping the Uno for a smaller Arduino Nano, adopting a higher-capacity Li-ion pack or external power supply, and streamlining the housing for better portability.

projects.title: Human Tracking Robotic Walking Table (Ongoing Project..)
projects.description: Assistive robotics for independence: Prototyping a Strandbeest-inspired human-tracking walking table that autonomously brings meds, drinks, and tools to the user—reducing reach/transfer risk and boosting day-to-day independence for people with mobility challenges—by engineering a Jansen-linkage gait with closed-loop person-following on Arduino Nano RP2040, driving a 24 V high-torque stepper via L298 dual H-bridge, and building a safe, modular power system (LiPo → Fankerba buck regulation, XT60 bus); an in-progress blend of art + control systems that turns static furniture into a helpful companion.

I was just moving, doing the next thing, staying busy. But I never had that one thing I believed in so hard that going home felt like quitting. Now I do. And I believe in it more than anyone. That means building Pesito and Todd all the way, I am going to because that’s who I am… I want to build something generational… Something that outlives me and changes the story for the people who come after me. So I’m betting everything on it. I’m 19 and I have way too much fun with everything I do. Some people don’t get that. Some people hate me for it. My Fidelity Investments internship ended in 1946. (Not a typo. Yooo LinkedIn Family!! storytime. 🥹✌️) My final week as an FCAT intern turned into a two-stop tour of an 80-year timeline. Stop one: the Fidelity archives in Merrimack. An archivist walked us through the company's history from the ground up, showing us the actual relics the founders and early employees used. Charts drawn by hand. Audits done on paper. Even the story behind Fidelity's frog!! Stop two: the Boston office, where I got up close with FCAT's technology and where Fidelity is heading next, consumer-facing tech, like virtual investing. Hand-drawn charts to virtual investing. Same company. Same mission. Different century. Standing in both rooms in the same week just hit different. Every relic in those archives was cutting edge once. And FCAT exists so the company that once drew charts by hand never stops building what's next. That's what I'm taking with me: technology doesn't stay still, and neither do the people who build it. If you're early in your career, that's the whole game, not mastering one tool, staying curious enough to build the next one. The hardest part about it all honestly? Saying goodbye to my team and the interns who turned two summers into something way bigger than an internship. If you know you know. 🤞 Two summers. One team. 80 years of proof that nothing worth building stays still. Whatever I build next… that's the standard yo✌️ ...more ...more

I was CREATIVELY inspired by Jocelyn V. ’s article on why she paid to return to ColorStack ’s Stacked Up Summit to put together my own breakdown, as someone who was there for the first time. I flew into San Francisco 8 months after joining ColorStack, only 3 months after becoming a member. Not only did feedback like hers, and countless others, shape how I prepared, but this summit turned out to be one of the greatest experiences of my time in ColorStack so far. I didn't wait to be ready, but that didn't mean I felt prepared, only that I wasn't willing to wait. I want to thank Viviana Ayala , my chapter's former and founding president, who not only introduced me to ColorStack but gave me just enough support to do it on my own. I also want to thank the people who made this weekend what it was. Keiyana Arnold, MSOM opened the day with energy (A LOT OF IT!) that carried the whole room. Then Arnell Calderon and Jehron W. Petty , president and CEO, took the stage, and that's when I realized the stranger from the bathroom was the CEO… Trust me, no one felt sillier than I did. Jeffrey Malcolm and Kay Malcolm followed with humor and raw meaning that stayed with me since (Kay Malcolm's line stuck with me the entire weekend: great work matters, so does visibility…). Equally impactful was the fireside chat with Dr. Miguel Angel Hernandez , Teresa Tyson , and Dr. Durryle Brooks, Ph.D, MA that made me think about my own experiences in the workplace. Some things didn't go as planned, but that ended up giving me more motivation. One of my favorite moments were with Ben-James (BJ) Brown who walked us through his path to Wells Fargo . What stood out was how much he loved what he did, and how much he wanted us to know it. I would like to thank once again Jocelyn Vazquez but also Jose Cruz-Lopez for their Campus to Career extensive resources, Arnell Calderon ’s networking tips, the ColorStack Slack community, and the people who made time to create and share their experience in the Level Up Series on YouTube that gave me the frameworks I built my whole approach around.
